81642.subject:
India's IT Industry Is Making Billions From AI. So Why Is Growth
 Still Under Pressure?
81642.body:
Ment Tech | Meant To Innovate

Автор: Ment Tech Labs


Автор: Ment Tech Labs

    
    
    Прочитайте цю статтю на LinkedIn, щоб приєднатися до обговорення
Прочитати на LinkedIn
https://www.linkedin.com/comm/pulse/indias-industry-making-billions-from-ai-so-why-growth-still-sbulf?lipi=urn%3Ali%3Apage%3Aemail_email_series_follow_newsletter_02%3BM9E5uW9oRgutvkjK5fvFdg%3D%3D&midToken=AQFTjFOONAfT2w&midSig=1jW6J5dXcJ4Yw1&trk=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_&trkEmail=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_-null-fz96fz~mvuuc78d~20-null-null&eid=fz96fz-mvuuc78d-20
  
October brought some impressive numbers from India's IT industry. On October 8, TCS reported $3.1 billion in annualised AI revenue. Two weeks later, Infosys revealed that its AI business had grown 29% in a single quarter. Sounds like the start of another IT boom, right? Not quite. TCS reported just 2.4% year-on-year dollar revenue growth. Infosys grew 1.5% in constant currency and cut its full-year growth forecast to 1–2%. Billions coming in from AI, yet overall growth is barely moving. For decades, India's IT companies made money by putting skilled engineers on projects and charging clients for their time. Now the same technology they're selling is helping clients get work done in fewer hours. And that's where things get complicated. The Numbers Don't Quite Add Up October's earnings reports tell the story better than any industry prediction. So, why isn't all that AI money showing up in overall growth? Part of the answer lies in cautious client spending and tougher pricing. Businesses are still investing in technology, but they're questioning every major expense. And when a project becomes cheaper to deliver, clients naturally want a share of the savings. The Problem With Selling Hours Imagine a software company that charged a client for ten developers working over three months. A year later, the same team has coding assistants, automated testing, and tools that handle much of the routine documentation. The project finishes earlier, the client is happy, and the developers are more productive. But when the next contract arrives, the client asks for a lower price. Fair question. Difficult answer. Indian IT companies spent years growing by adding engineers to projects. Under hourly contracts, fewer working hours can mean less revenue. Fixed-price projects work differently, though. Finishing early can actually improve profits. Same technology. Two very different outcomes. A faster project doesn't always mean a bigger invoice. Sometimes, it means exactly the opposite. That's the uncomfortable reality the industry now has to deal with. Clients Aren't Looking for Another Chatbot Walk into a bank, hospital, or retail business, and you'll probably find work that still takes far too long. Bank employees checking customer documents, hospital staff answering the same questions, or retail teams struggling with inventory records.

## ChatGPT's new rules come with bodyguards

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/1672f514-1449-4471-9fb1-19e952d27f2a/Oct_30_-_1.jpg?t=1793350323)
Caption: 

OpenAI just [rewrote its Model Spec](https://openai.com/index/updated-model-spec/), the public rulebook for how ChatGPT should behave. It now focuses on five values: following human intent, minimizing harm, honesty, human agency, and care.

The company also revealed how it monitors its most powerful AI agents to catch suspicious behavior, including attempts to escape their testing environments.

* OpenAI replayed an earlier security incident and found that its new monitors would have raised an alert more than 30 hours before the actual breach.

* In a separate live training run, the monitors caught an AI model accessing the internet without permission within 15 minutes.

* Serious alerts go to human security teams, and some critical incidents can automatically pause the affected AI activity.

The 30-hour finding came from replaying an old incident, not catching it live.

OpenAI admits its models don't fully follow the new rulebook yet, and the monitoring system still has weaknesses. The company is writing rules for its AI while building ways to catch it when it breaks them.

View this post on the web at https://linas.substack.com/p/yc-winter-2027-requests-for-startups

👋 Hey, Linas here! Every day, I break down 3 stories shaping the future of FinTech & Artificial Intelligence - plus the money movements and trends worth tracking. First time here? 400k+ FinTech and AI leaders get this daily. Join them:
Y Combinator’s Winter 2027 Requests for Startups (RFS) opens with one sentence: “AI’s biggest bottlenecks are moving beyond the models.”
The 11 requests cover space access, the US robot supply chain, data center equipment, financing for physical AI, government benefits verification, city permitting, air-gapped AI, owned and vertical foundation models, AI-backed expert services and models that write well.
Read together, they make one argument. Intelligence is getting cheap. Steel, magnets, transformers, permits, verified data, capital and trust are not. YC is betting that the next cycle’s biggest companies will be built where AI runs into those constraints. The money already agrees. AI took $102B of the $159B in global venture funding in Q3 2026 (see below), and hyperscalers are on track to spend about $1T on capex this year.
The openings YC describes sit in the gaps around the companies raising $1 billion rounds: the actuator a humanoid maker can no longer import, or the Medicaid renewal a state can’t process by hand. Several of those gaps come with deadlines attached, and the first arrives in January 2027.
1. What changed in YC’s Winter 2027 RFS
From AI apps to AI bottlenecks
The previous list was still mostly about AI products. Fall 2026 included Multiplayer AI, a Cloud for Small Software, AI consumer products for a billion people, AI for the aging population, crypto, and Proving You’re Human.
Winter 2027 moves down the stack. Consumer apps are gone, apart from one request about how models write. And YC isn’t the only firm reading the market this way. Founder read: mega-rounds are going to a small number of companies. A capex boom this size also has a real financing problem, and the companies writing the checks won’t solve it for the suppliers and lenders around them.
Those numbers explain why YC wrote this list now. For each of the 11 requests, we checked YC’s claims against the latest data and paired them with three startup ideas you could start pitching this quarter.
